html:
Sogdia, or Sogdiana, was the ancient land of the Sogdians in Central Asia, between the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, around Samarkand and Bukhara in today's Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. Its Iranian-speaking merchants were the great middlemen of the Silk Road from about 300 to 800 CE.

Sogdia was a province of the Achaemenid Empire. Alexander the Great spent two hard years subduing it, married Roxana, the daughter of a local noble, and founded Alexandria Eschate on its northern edge. It was rarely one state: its cities had their own lords, usually under some outside overlord, Kushan, Hephthalite or Turkic.

Sogdian merchants built colonies along the roads to China. The Sogdian Ancient Letters, lost in the early 300s near Dunhuang, are mail between them, and the Afrasiyab murals in Samarkand show envoys from as far as China and Korea. They carried Manichaeism and Buddhism east, and their script is the ancestor of the Uyghur and Mongolian scripts. An Lushan, whose rebellion shook Tang China from 755, was of Sogdian descent. After the Arab conquest in the early 700s Sogdia slowly became Muslim and Persian-speaking.
